items.title: Choropleth maps show areal data; isoline maps show continuous data
items.claim: What is the difference between choropleth and isoline maps?

options.text: There is no difference — alternative names for the same thing
Choropleth: defined areas (countries, counties) shaded by category. Isoline: lines connecting points of equal value (contours, isobars, isotherms, isohyets)
Isoline maps cannot show climate data

items.reveal:
Choropleth maps assume uniform values within each area; they are vulnerable to the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) — different boundary choices produce different patterns.

Isoline maps (also called isarithmic) treat the variable as a continuous surface. Examples: contour lines (relief), isobars (atmospheric pressure), isotherms (temperature), isohyets (rainfall).

Other techniques: dot maps (each dot represents a count), proportional symbols (size scaled to value), flow lines (volume of movement), cartograms (areas distorted by value).
items.why: Map technique matters. The same data, mapped differently, tells different stories — and the right technique depends on whether the underlying variable is areal or continuous.

items.title: Spearman's rank correlation goes from -1 to +1
items.claim: What does Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measure?

options.text: The strength and direction of monotonic association between ranked variables, between -1 (perfect negative) and +1 (perfect positive); 0 indicates no monotonic relationship
The mean of the two variables

items.reveal:
Spearman's ρ uses ranks rather than raw values, making it robust to outliers and non-linear monotonic relationships. Pearson's r requires a linear relationship and normally-distributed data.

Critical values must be checked against sample size: with n=10, ρ must exceed about 0.564 to be significant at p=0.05. With n=30, the threshold is about 0.306.

A strong correlation can be coincidental, confounded by a third variable, or reversed in direction (Simpson's paradox). 'Correlation does not imply causation' is a methodological starting point, not a slogan.
items.why: Statistical reasoning is part of geographical skills. Strong correlation is evidence, not proof — geographers must argue causation separately from association, ideally through mechanism.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — southern England is sinking
items.claim: What is glacial isostatic adjustment in the British Isles?

options.text: Britain has fully recovered from the Ice Age

Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England subside by around 1 mm/year as the forebulge collapses — both measured directly by GPS
The motion is too slow to measure

items.reveal:
When the British-Irish Ice Sheet melted (around 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rebound. Because the mantle behaves viscously over thousand-year timescales, the response is still ongoing.

The British Isles GNSS Facility (BIGF) measures vertical motion directly. Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or in some places falling) relative sea level.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rebounding even faster — up to 10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia. The Baltic Sea is gradually shrinking on the Scandinavian side.
items.why: Sea-level projections combine global climate signal with local geophysics. The Thames Barrier defends a coast that is itself sinking — accelerating the apparent rise.
